newsitem.title: FRANCE: France presses Renault to talk on closure.
newsitem.headline: France presses Renault to talk on closure.

text.p: The French government, anxious to avert a European crisis and serious labour unrest, intervened on Wednesday in the growing furore over car maker Renault SA's decision to shut its Belgian assembly plan, axing 3,100 jobs.

Without challenging the industrial logic, Prime Minister Alain Juppe summoned Renault's chairman to complain about the way the move had been handled and demanded that the firm open immediate talks with the Belgian workforce and authorities.
Under pressure from Paris, Brussels and the European Commission, Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said he was ready to discuss "converting" the Vilvoorde plant near Brussels.

He pledged that Renault, expected to announce heavy losses later this month, would fully respect French, Belgian and European regulations in its restructuring plans, which also involve more than 2,700 job cuts in France this year.
The decision to close Vilvoorde in June triggered widespread protests in Belgium, political anger on both sides of the border and the beginnings of a boycott of Renault vehicles in Belgium.

"I told the prime minister that Renault wants to start consultations immediately with representatives of the personnel at Vilvoorde about accompanying measures and the possibilities of converting the factory," Schweitzer said. He did not say to what alternative use the plant might be put.
President Jacques Chirac earlier told the French cabinet he was shocked by the method used by Renault, which is still 46 percent state-owned.
French media questioned the government's sudden indignation, saying it had been aware of Renault's plans since mid-January but had studiously kept its distance from the decision.

Juppe said in a statement he had asked Schweitzer to open consultations without delay under Belgian and EU law and would inform Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde, of the outcome of the meeting.
Schweitzer said he would present the restructuring plan to Renault's works council on Thursday and hold a special European works council on March 11, including Belgian staff delegates.

The French government's intervention was an abrupt change in tactics reflecting apparent concern at the damage to France's image and interests in Belgium and beyond, and at the risk of industrial unrest spreading to France.
Trade unions have called a one-hour work stoppage at Renault factories across Europe on Friday.

Several hundred Belgian Renault employees facing redundancy drove to France to picket a Renault factory at Douai, south of Lille and staged a joint demonstration with French trade unionists, who declared solidarity with their Belgian comrades.
In Vilvoorde, sirens sounded, traffic stopped and citizens observed five minutes' silence in protest at the closure, while a black flag hung from the town hall.

In Brussels, European Commission President Jacques Santer accused Renault of violating the spirit of European legislation and appeared to encourage planned lawsuits against the firm by the Belgian and Flanders regional governments.

French Industry Minister Franck Borotra acknowledged that Renault had informed the French and Belgian governments in advance of the decision to close Vilvoorde. He said it was a few days before the official announcement.

However the newspaper Le Monde said Juppe's office had known about the Renault plan since mid-January. Privatised in two stages in 1994 and 1996, Renault has 138,000 employees. The state still has representatives on its supervisory board.
Borotra told Europe 1 radio that Schweitzer had come to see him a few days before the Vilvoorde decision was announced.
"I told him -- you take your responsibility and as a shareholder I will judge your policy by its results," he said.
Asked if Dehaene, who has bitterly attacked the Renault move, was informed in advance, Borotra said: "Of course, in the days before the announcement."
Dehaene confirmed he had been told of the possible closure a week before the announcement but he said he had said the idea must be ruled out.
Borotra said the decision to close Vilvoorde was necessary to reduce costs and respond to competition. "Restructurings cannot be avoided," he said, adding "even Renault can die".
